summary.text: A convergent boundary is a place where two or more of Earth's lithospheric plates collide, and one plate eventually slides beneath the other in a process called subduction.
These collisions play out over millions to tens of millions of years and can bring volcanoes, earthquakes, mountain building and the destruction of lithosphere.
As a cool slab sinks and heats up, its minerals release water into the hotter asthenosphere, causing partial melting that can feed volcanic arcs at the surface.

items.prompt: Two slabs of ocean floor collide. One has had a long time to cool; the other is still warm. Which one ends up going under?

options.label: The warm one, since heat makes rock soft
The cool one, since it is denser
Neither; they crumple into a mountain
Whichever slab is moving faster

items.explain: In ocean-to-ocean collisions the cooler, denser lithosphere sinks beneath the warmer, less dense lithosphere.

items.prompt: Volcanoes line up above a slab of seafloor sinking into the mantle. What mainly lets rock melt there?

options.label: Friction heat from plates grinding together
Molten iron rising straight from the core
Water from the slab lowering the melting point
The slab itself melting from surface heat

items.explain: Heating breaks down water-bearing minerals in the sinking slab, and that water lowers the melting temperature of the surrounding mantle rock so it partly melts.

items.prompt: Two continents drift toward each other until they meet head-on. What happens at the meeting line?

options.label: One continent dives deep like ocean floor
The two pull apart and open a new ocean
They slide smoothly past each other sideways
Neither sinks far, since continental rock is buoyant

items.explain: Continental lithosphere is buoyant and resists sinking beneath other continental lithosphere, so neither continental plate subducts.

items.prompt: Deep-sea mud rides on an ocean plate toward a continent, where the plate dives under. Where does much of that mud end up?

options.label: Scraped off and piled onto the continent's edge
Carried down intact all the way to the core
Melted at once into lava at the trench
Pushed back toward the ridge it came from

items.explain: As the oceanic plate subducts, deep-sea sediments and some oceanic crust are scraped off and build a wedge on the continental crust.

items.prompt: Earthquakes cluster where one plate dives under another. How deep have such earthquakes been detected?

options.label: About 10 km
About 70 km
About 670 km
About 3,000 km

items.explain: Earthquakes in subduction zones have been detected as deep as 670 km.

items.prompt: Once a slab of old seafloor starts sliding down into the mantle, what helps keep pulling it deeper?

options.label: Gravity acting on the cold, dense slab
Magnetic pull from Earth's iron core
The Moon's tides dragging on the plate
Pressure from the volcanoes above it

items.explain: The cold, dense subducting plate is pulled into the mantle, with gravity helping to drive it down.
